Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the AeroDef Dynamics Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, the Q&A session will follow the standard operator instructions for queuing and unmuting. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to AeroDef Dynamics' Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Elena Vasquez, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Thornton, Chief Operating Officer; Dr. Lisa Chen, Chief Technology Officer; and Robert Kline, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those statements.

Johnathan Hale:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. AeroDef Dynamics delivered a solid performance in the third quarter, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, commercial aerospace, and advanced systems. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering long-term value to our shareholders.

One of the strongest indicators of our long-term revenue visibility is our backlog, which isn't just a number—it's a multi-year pipeline of funded and unfunded orders reflecting deep customer commitments amid geopolitical volatility, supply chain normalization, and surging demand for next-generation capabilities. At quarter-end, our total backlog reached $142.3 billion, an absolute increase of $21.7 billion, representing robust 18% year-over-year growth from $120.6 billion at the end of Q3 2023. Quarter-over-quarter, we grew by $4.2 billion, or 3.1%, from Q2's $138.1 billion level. This delivers a trailing twelve-month book-to-bill ratio of 1.25x, comfortably above the 1.0x breakeven that signals sustained organic growth.

Breaking it down by our core segments reveals differentiated drivers. In defense, backlog hit $108.5 billion, up $19.2 billion or 21% year-over-year, powered by U.S. Department of Defense multi-year procurement contracts and international Foreign Military Sales. Key wins this quarter included a $4.8 billion fixed-price contract for Lot 16 F-35 low-rate initial production aircraft, building on the Joint Strike Fighter program's momentum where we've secured positions on more than 1,200 jets delivered across 19 operators to date. We also captured $2.1 billion in orders for hypersonic boost-glide vehicles under the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon program, leveraging FY24 supplemental appropriations in response to tensions in Ukraine and the Indo-Pacific. Unfunded options now stand at $45 billion, including indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity task orders for our Next Generation Air Dominance digital engineering demonstrators. Regionally, U.S. DoD accounts for 72%, EMEA grew 25% on F-35 exports to NATO allies like Poland and Finland, and Asia-Pacific expanded 35% via sustainment deals for allied F-16 upgrades.

Commercial aerospace backlog climbed to $24.6 billion, up $1.9 billion or 8% year-over-year from $22.7 billion, as post-pandemic recovery gains traction with narrowbody demand outpacing widebodies. Highlights encompassed $1.2 billion in orders for 737 MAX derivative wing assemblies, supporting Boeing's planned ramp to 38 per month by 2025, plus $450 million from Airbus A320neo family pylon contracts. While supply chain challenges linger, our tier-1 supplier role with both OEMs yielded a 1.1x book-to-bill. APAC airlines such as IndiGo and AirAsia drove 40% of new bookings, tied to fleet modernization for intra-Asia traffic forecasted at a 6% CAGR through 2030 according to IATA.

Space and advanced systems backlog advanced to $9.2 billion, a $450 million or 5% year-over-year gain, riding the commercial space surge and national security priorities. Standouts were $800 million for payload integration on 12 ULA Vulcan Centaur launches under the National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 1 contract, helping us compete with SpaceX's Starship ambitions, and $300 million for proliferated LEO satellite constellations in the Space Development Agency's Tranche 2 Transport Layer. We also progressed directed energy laser systems, securing $150 million for HELIOS pod integration on U.S. Navy destroyers. International exposure is 28%, spearheaded by European Space Agency partnerships for Ariane 6 upper stages.

This backlog expansion highlights three strategic thrusts. Our $2.5 billion R&D commitment to digital twins and model-based systems engineering has sped contract wins, cutting proposal-to-award cycles by 30% on Joint All-Domain Command and Control programs. Inflation safeguards through economic price adjustment clauses in 85% of DoD fixed-price contracts protected margins, converting $3.2 billion in FY24 options to funded backlog. We're also managing concurrency risks effectively, with our F-35 production ratio under 2.5:1 per GAO standards, sidestepping certification pitfalls akin to the Boeing 737 MAX.

Looking ahead, tailwinds include the proposed FY25 National Defense Authorization Act's $886 billion topline, Ukraine and Israel supplementals potentially adding $20-30 billion industry-wide, and commercial aftermarket rebound as CFM LEAP engine shop visits accelerate. Near-term risks involve DoD continuing resolution uncertainty and titanium constraints from Russia sanctions, but our diversified $142 billion backlog—65% funded—offers outstanding visibility through 2030, backing our raised FY24 revenue guidance of $28-29 billion and EPS of $12.50-$13.00.

We are particularly excited about recent advancements in our hypersonic boost-glide vehicle program and its potential to solidify our leadership in next-gen defense capabilities for future growth. Demand for our defense systems remains strong, and our commercial aerospace business continues its steady recovery.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Johnathan. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $26.4 billion, representing a 9% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $3.25. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $12 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year has been raised, as Johnathan noted. We are actively managing costs while investing in key growth initiatives and remain committed to returning capital to shareholders through our dividend and a $500 million share repurchase program this year.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 22.3%, operating income of $3.0 billion, and free cash flow of $2.0 billion.

Before moving on, I'd like to provide deeper insight into our revenue drivers and headwinds for the quarter, giving you the context on what's fueling top-line momentum and the obstacles we're addressing. While Johnathan covered the backlog foundation, this quarter's results underscore the durability of our $142 billion backlog, up 18% year-over-year, with a book-to-bill of 1.25x.

Our key revenue drivers fall into three pillars: defense systems, commercial aerospace, and emerging technologies. Defense is our cornerstone, contributing 62% of revenue at $16.4 billion, up 22% year-over-year. This stemmed from ramped deliveries on hypersonic weapons, where we increased production to 18 units per quarter from 12 a year ago on programs akin to the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, ahead of USAF Lot 3 awards. Geopolitical pressures in the Indo-Pacific and Europe boosted demand, with Indo-Pacific sales jumping 35% to $4.2 billion on F-35 sustainment for allies like Japan and Australia, featuring Block 4 upgrades with advanced electronic warfare suites and distributed aperture systems.

Missiles and precision munitions shone, generating $6.5 billion up 28%, driven by Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile Extended Range and Long Range Anti-Ship Missile replenishments amid Ukraine drawdowns. DoD FY24 budget reconciliation at $886 billion unlocked $2.1 billion in new task orders since January, including Next Generation Air Dominance risk reduction, pushing book-to-bill to 1.4x with FY25 visibility via NDAA great-power competition focus.

Commercial aerospace, 28% of revenue at $7.4 billion up 12% year-over-year, benefits from post-pandemic rebound. Narrowbody ramps on Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo content spanned nacelles and thrust reversers for over 450 aircraft deliveries year-to-date. Aftermarket services, our 45% EBITDA margin gem, grew 19% to $3.2 billion on elevated flight hours—global revenue passenger kilometers now 105% of 2019 per IATA. Our GE Aviation tie-up on the CFM RISE open-fan architecture secured a $1.2 billion framework for 15% content on future narrowbody engines.

Emerging technologies, 10% at $2.6 billion up 35%, powers growth. Space systems reached $1.5 billion via Vulcan Centaur payload fairings for United Launch Alliance and DARPA Blackjack-like responsive space demos. Uncrewed systems, Group 5 UAS successors to the RQ-4 Global Hawk, added $1.3 billion from Army Multi-Domain Operations prototypes. We're allocating 8% of revenue, or $2.1 billion, to FY24 R&D in AI/machine learning autonomy and proprietary ceramic matrix composites for hypersonic reentry vehicles.

On headwinds, which compressed segment margins to 22.3% from 23.1%, supply chain issues drove 60% of $1.8 billion cost variances. Titanium forgings face constraints from Ukraine suppliers, with spot prices up 25% year-over-year, delaying F-35 wing skins 4-6 weeks. Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan durability on A320neos deferred 15% of aftermarket into H2. We've countered with dual-sourcing—40% titanium now U.S. and Australian—and qualifying expanded composites capacity.

Labor inflation hit $900 million, skilled trades premiums 15-20% at Oklahoma and Alabama sites, amid sector wage growth of 5.2% per Deloitte. Retention bonuses and apprenticeships held turnover at 4.2% versus industry 6.8%. Program costs grew on B-21 Raider low-rate production by $500 million from learning curves; we're negotiating equitable adjustments under Federal Acquisition Regulation.

Regionally, North America was 72% at $19 billion on U.S. government spend, Europe 15% at $4.2 billion hampered by Airbus ripples and Future Combat Air System funding delays, Asia-Pacific 10% at $2.6 billion brightened by India's Tejas Mk2 offsets despite China rare earth controls hiking actuator magnet costs 18%, and Middle East/LATAM 3% steady but cyclical.

We're mitigating aggressively: Digital Supply Chain with blockchain traceability and analytics trimmed lead times 22%, additive manufacturing internalized 30% titanium parts for 15% savings, and sustainability via SAF composites and hybrid-electric rotorcraft for low-boom programs. FY25 DoD $849.8 billion base favors 5th-gen and space, Boeing stabilizing at 38 737s monthly. Risks like continuing resolutions delaying $8 billion awards or recession trimming aftermarket persist, but 85% of 2025 revenue contracted and margins to 23-24% position us for 12-15% organic growth.

Next, on our updated full-year 2024 guidance, which we're raising today on strong execution, program accelerations, and demand from defense and commercial. Previously $14.8-15.2 billion revenue and $7.80-8.20 adjusted EPS; now revenue $15.6-16.0 billion, 8% growth at midpoint, and EPS $8.50-8.90, 12% growth.

By segment: Defense systems 65% to $10.2-10.5 billion on hypersonics like our GAD-400 glide vehicle with scramjet, Block 4 Javelin successors via FMS to Ukraine; margins to 14.5% via digital twins at Huntsville. Commercial 25% to $3.9-4.1 billion on 737 MAX/A320neo winglets at 120% plan, SAF nacelles for 15% drag cut on LEAPs. Space/advanced 10% to $1.5-1.6 billion on Orion modules for Artemis IV, Space Force SATCOM, HELIOS lasers at TRL 8.

Regions: U.S. gov 55% on $886 billion NDAA hypersonics/F-35 LRIP 16; international 30% with Poland Patriot MSE, UAE/Saudi THAAD, Asia drones; commercial OEMs 15%.

Metrics: Operating margins 12.0-12.5% via AI PLM overhead cuts 10%, pricing; EPS from $250 million pension, low interest on $3 billion cash. FCF $1.4-1.6 billion for $1.1 billion repurchases, 20% dividend to $2.40. Capex $450 million on additive for F-35, Wichita expansion. Backlog $28 billion 1.8x revenue, 40% options; hedged supply, geopol upside $200 million surge clauses. Assumes stable macro, no Boeing probes impact; 'Tech-for-Threat' R&D 8% for 6th-gen, quantum, autonomy in $2.5 trillion market.

Now, segment revenues for Q3: consolidated $26.4 billion up 9%, book-to-bill 1.15x, backlog record providing multi-year sightlines with air travel and geopol tailwinds.

Commercial aerospace $11.2 billion, +18% YoY, 42% total. Post-pandemic traffic exceeding 2019 by 5-7% through 2025 per IATA, titanium easing. OEM 185 narrowbody ships +25%, 737 MAX/A320neo ramps, 1,200 engines incl GE9X for 777X. Offset Pratt GTF inspections via MRO hubs. North America 55% U.S. LCCs, Europe +22% Ryanair/easyJet, APAC +28% IndiGo. $1.2 billion additive/digital twins for 200 bps margins by FY26; backlog $78 billion 1.3x book-to-bill for 12-15% CAGR SAF era.

Defense $11.8 billion +4% YoY, 45%, $92 billion backlog. DoD +6% FY24, Ukraine/Indo-Pacific supplementals. Missiles $4.1 billion +12% JASSM-ER/LRASM/hypersonics 1,500 units NATO restock. Fixed-wing +5% F-35 sustain $2.8 billion +8% 156/year Lot 15. Rotary/space flat NGAD delays, but EW NGJ-MB-like $1.5 billion IDIQ. U.S. 72% +3%, intl +9% Middle East Patriot +15%, Europe F-35 +12%. AI sensor fusion CCA drones Q1 2025 flight; margins 12.4%, FY25 $923 billion NDAA low-double-digit.

Services $3.4 billion +14% YoY, 13%, 22.1% margins top. Flight hours +8% 1.2 trillion ASMs Cirium. MRO +16% CFM56/LEAP overhauls American/Lufthansa, components +11% TrueChoice-like. Defense services 35% +10% F-35 ALIS/ODIN Black Hawk. EMEA +17% Dubai/Frankfurt, APAC +15% SE Asia LCCs. $500 million digital AR/PHM Blade Watch to 75% take rates; backlog $15 billion five-year recurring.

This balance shows resilience, on track FY $102-105 billion revenue 11-12% margins, Q4 sequential uptick.

Michael Thornton:
Thank you, Elena. Operationally, we've achieved major gains in supply chain management, boosting production rates on flagship programs. Investments in automation, digital technologies, and dual-sourcing have enhanced efficiency, cut costs, and shortened lead times by over 20%. Dual titanium mills and blockchain traceability have stabilized inputs, while apprenticeship programs keep skilled labor turnover low.

Dr. Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Michael. Technologically, we're advancing next-generation propulsion systems, including scramjet-enabled hypersonics and high-bypass turbofans. These innovations, combined with AI autonomy and ceramic matrix composites, will deliver competitive edges in hypersonics, uncrewed systems, and sustainable aviation. Our directed energy lasers and proliferated LEO payloads are hitting milestones ahead of schedule.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Hunter Carter with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Hunter Carter:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the commercial aircraft delivery rates and recovery trajectory?

Johnathan Hale:
Certainly, Hunter. As a cornerstone of our growth, our commercial aviation segment demands a close look at delivery performance and recovery dynamics. In Q3, we achieved 128 commercial aircraft deliveries, lifting year-to-date to 245 units—a 28% year-over-year rise from 191 in first half 2023, outpacing our full-year midpoint of 520. Narrowbodies dominated at 82% with 105 Falcon 9000-series and Eagle 7000X units, widebodies at 23 including five Titan 500 ultra-long-range.

Pre-COVID peaks hit 52 monthly across portfolio in Q4 2019 on 737 MAX/A320neo surges; pandemic lows were 12 monthly Q2 2020 amid $10 billion OEM cash burn. Now V-shaped, monthly rates from 35 Q4 2022 to 42 Q3 average, June 46 post-pandemic high. Record backlog 4,800 aircraft ~$425 billion list, +8% year-end 2023, over eight years at current rates, 65% narrowbody high-margin.

Trends favor efficient platforms: Falcon 9000 (737 MAX equiv LEAP-1B) 60% Q3 deliveries ramping 4% monthly post-FAA software nods; Titan 500 (777X rival) +50% YoY GE9X certs. SAF certs 15% Q3 for CORSIA/net-zero like Delta/Emirates.

Regions: North America 38% (49 Q3) United/Southwest domestic RPK +12% IATA; APAC 32% (41) IndiGo/AirAsia X 22 units intra-Asia 95% 2019; Europe 18% (23) Ryanair/easyJet Spirit-like issues but Lufthansa 10 Eagle order; Middle East/LATAM Qatar FIFA pull-forwards.

Headwinds: machined/avionics Collins/Honeywell delays cap widebody 80%, Everett/Renton labor +2-3 week cycles despite $500 million automation. GE/Pratt bottlenecks, GTF A320neo ripples; dual CFM sourcing helps.

Execution: $2.8 billion capex doubles Falcon line 38-52/month mid-2026 digital twins/AI F-35 proven; Spirit JV fuselages -25% leads, Safran hybrid APUs 2030. Defense synergies titanium C-17 to comm -8% costs, RQ-4 ISR to avionics.

Guidance: FY24 500-550 deliveries H2 255-305 monthly 45-50; 2025 650 +25% wide 6 narrow 48; 2030 900 35% single-aisle $4.5 trillion Cirium. Pricing discounts 55% list vs pre-50%; risks APAC geopol/recession 10-15% defer. Margins +220 bps to 12.1% Q3, more leverage ahead. Resilient reacceleration.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Jenkins with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins:
Hi, thanks. I wanted to dive into your forward-looking view on risks and opportunities. With guidance raised, can you unpack key macro headwinds, program exposures, and upside levers in the backlog or new bids?

Elena Vasquez:
Thanks, Sarah, good morning. As always, forward-looking matters including risks and opportunities are subject to our 10-K and 10-Q filings—actuals could vary on geopolitics, supply chains, regulations, funding shifts.

Framing by segments—Aerospace Platforms 45% FY revenue, Defense Systems 35%, Space/Advanced 20%—with $142.3 billion Q3 backlog up 18%. Robust demand from security needs, but challenges abound. Opportunities first, then risks, with positioning strategies.

Opportunities center on hypersonics, autonomy, international. Global A&D to $1.1 trillion 5.8% CAGR Deloitte 2030 great-power/modernization. Our hypersonic/autonomous pipeline 25% funded backlog vs 18% last year.

ARROW-6 glide for Army LRHW: $2.4 billion Q1 mod, FY26 IOC, White Sands Mach 7+ 95% hit vs AGM-183A setbacks; $1-2 billion annual FY28 on $14.5 billion DoD R&D.

Autonomy ViperDrone Group 3 UAS AI swarms: 1,200 Ukraine FMS $450 million, 8+ hour loiter 92% success CENTCOM; Indo-Pacific $1.8 billion JMSDF anti-sub AUKUS; APAC 22% intl vs 15% FY22, India MRFA F-36 shortlist $15 billion 36-72 units.

Space OrionStar 48 LEO SpaceX PWSA missile warning $320 million Q2 +28%, $3.1 billion backlog; $150 million FY24 digital twins MBSE -40% cycles vs Northrop B-21 software.

Commercial 737 MAX/A320neo +18% titanium/composites, SAF United; 15% commercial FY26 vs DoD risks.

M&A cyber $1.2 billion powder; Siemens NX/ANSYS -25% proto for NGAD bids.

Risks: Geopol Taiwan/Middle East +/-20% models; Ukraine $1.1 billion sales FY22 but election CRs 10-15% defer $4.2 billion DoD, worst $500 million FY25 hit.

Supply: Pratt PW1100G idles 20% F-36, titanium +35% sanctions margin squeeze MQ-25 5-7% growth; 75% force majeure, US/Kazakh hedge Q4 FY25 norm; labor 12% inflation hypersonics engineers attrition 4.2% $50 million Purdue upskill.

DEW HELIOS DDG-51 150-300kW $300 million overrun risk FPD 22% backlog 95/5 traps KC-46 like.

ITAR 6-month lags, FAA eVTOL $200 million defer; cyber 3x probes Q2 $80 million zero-trust.

Europe Zeitenwende +$100 billion but UK cuts Typhoon 10%; Middle East 12% volatile Iran; China bans 5% vs 7% growth.

Mitigations: intl backlog 38% vs 32%, cost discipline EBITDA 14.5-15.5% 200bps gross digital; $12 billion liquidity inflation 4.5%; upside Golden Dome/SDA EGS $5-7 billion FY26 EPS +15%.

Opportunities outweigh risks 2:1 base, FY24 9-11% growth solid. Resilient tech-forward execution.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Ross with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Ross:
Thanks. Regarding the advancements in next-gen propulsion and hypersonics?

Dr. Lisa Chen:
Emily, great question. Our propulsion breakthroughs, from scramjet hypersonics achieving Mach 7+ with high hit rates to high-bypass fans like GE9X equivalents, integrate CMC materials and AI autonomy. HELIOS lasers at TRL 8 for counter-UAS, proliferated LEO for resilient SATCOM, and NGAD demonstrators position us ahead. R&D focus accelerates these for competitive dominance.

Johnathan Hale:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call. Slides and replay details are on our investor relations site.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
